newsitem.title: USA: US Feb durable goods add to fears of May rate hike.
newsitem.headline: US Feb durable goods add to fears of May rate hike.

text.p: February's robust strength in the U.S. manufacturing sector, which caught the bond market offguard Wednesday, has led many market analysts to believe yet another short-term interest rate rise could come in May.
The Commerce Department said durable goods orders rose 1.5 percent in February compared to an upwardly revised 4.1 percent increase in January.
U.S. economists in a Reuters survey had expected, on average, a 0.4-percent decline in orders after January's healthy jump.

Analysts had been expecting a slight pullback in February to follow January's strong numbers. But the report, and the upward revision in last month's data, surprised experts and signaled continued strength in manufacturing.
"It suggests manufacturing is gearing up for a great year," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc.

John Williams, chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust Co, agreed, adding the data "suggest more tightening moves down the road. There has been no evidence in this report of a slowdown in the economy."
The report showing a healthy manufacturing sector came just a day after the Federal Reserve hiked a key short-term interest rate, citing "persisting strength in demand" in the U.S. economy.
The federal funds rate was lifted by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent.
Robert McGee, senior economist at Tokai Bank Ltd, said the durable goods report "sort of validates the Fed's feeling the economy is likely to overheat if they don't exercise a little restraint."

The data showed across-the-board growth, with the strongest rise coming in orders for electronic and electrical equipment, up 7.4 percent to $30.6 billion. Only the transportation sector slipped in February.
Also noted by experts was an increase in shipments of finished products and order backlogs, which rose for the ninth time in ten months.
"This confirms that the U.S. economy is running at a pace that is unsustainably strong," said Bankers Trust's Williams.

The report spooked the bond market, sending Treasuries lower and pushing up the yield on the long bond briefly to seven percent. At 1020 EST/1520 GMT the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was off ten basis points to yield 6.99 percent.

Analysts said the seven percent level was likely to hold for now, but Williams said 7.25 percent "is manifest destiny" if the beginning of the second fiscal quarter shows the same clear signs of growth as the first quarter.
Although the data push the odds of another Fed tightening a bit higher, another rise in rates at the Fed policy committee's meeting on May 20 is by no means a sure thing, analysts said.
Other factors, including the strength of the dollar and a slew of economic reports, will be scrutinized in the weeks before the meeting.

"A big question is what happens in durable goods next month. It will show us if (February) was a sign of strength or just a volatile number. If it wasn't just an aberration, (the Fed) will probably do something" in May," said A.G. Edwards' Thayer.
